t: Number of Subarrays With AND Value of K
o: For each right endpoint we need the count of left endpoints where the AND of nums[l..r] equals k. The key fact: as l decreases, the AND of nums[l..r] is non-increasing in bits, so the set of distinct AND values ending at index r has at most ~20 elements (each step removes at least one bit). Maintain this small list with counts and sum the counts of entries equal to k.
k: Distinct suffix-AND values ending at any index number at most log(max) ≈ 20, because AND-ing can only clear bits.
Extend the list by AND-ing every previous distinct value with the new element, merging duplicates.
Sum counts of entries equal to k for each right endpoint.

a.n: Approach 1: Distinct-AND list per right endpoint
a.i: cur holds pairs (AND value, count of left endpoints producing it) for subarrays ending at the current index. Adding nums[r] maps every old value v to v & nums[r]; identical results merge, keeping the list logarithmic.
s: For each x in nums: start a new list with (x, 1).
For each (v, c) in the previous list: w = v & x; append/merge (w, c).
Add to the answer the total count of entries whose value equals k.
Replace the old list and continue.
a.t: O(n log max) — each right endpoint processes a list of at most ~30 distinct AND values
a.sp: O(log max) for the current list

a.n: Approach 2: Sparse-table binary search on AND breakpoints
a.i: Precompute a sparse table for range AND. For a fixed right endpoint r, the AND over [l..r] is monotone non-increasing as l decreases and takes O(log) distinct values; binary search each breakpoint with range-AND queries and count lengths where the value equals k.
s: Build sparse table for O(1) range AND.
For each r, find breakpoints of the distinct AND values via binary search on l.
For each segment where AND == k, add its length to the answer.

c.python:
class Solution:
    def countSubarrays(self, nums, k):
        n = len(nums)
        LOG = max(1, n.bit_length())
        sp = [nums[:]]
        j = 1
        while (1 << j) <= n:
            prev = sp[-1]
            sp.append([prev[i] & prev[i + (1 << (j-1))] for i in range(n - (1 << j) + 1)])
            j += 1
        def qry(l, r):
            j = (r - l + 1).bit_length() - 1
            return sp[j][l] & sp[j][r - (1 << j) + 1]
        ans = 0
        for r in range(n):
            l = r
            while l >= 0:
                v = qry(l, r)
                lo, hi = 0, l
                while lo < hi:
                    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
                    if qry(mid, r) == v: hi = mid
                    else: lo = mid + 1
                if v == k: ans += l - lo + 1
                l = lo - 1
        return ans

a.t: O(n log² n) — per right endpoint, O(log) segments each found by binary search with O(1) queries
a.sp: O(n log n) for the sparse table

w: Approach 1 is the intended optimal solution — short, cache-friendly, and hard to get wrong. Beware k = 0 (empty-AND semantics don't exist here; a subarray always has a defined AND) and use 64-bit accumulation since the answer can reach n(n+1)/2 ≈ 5e9. Follow-up: count subarrays with OR = k (symmetric technique) or AND > k (offline with a trie).
